title: Review: Chemistry — The particulate nature of matter
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C1#c14 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C1#c10 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C1#c05 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C1.1#xt2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C1#q01, C1#x04 (written for the game), C1#q04, C1#q09, C1#q07, C1#q14, C1#q06, C1#q13, C1#x01 (written for the game), C1#q10, C1#x02 (written for the game), C1#x03 (written for the game). The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Condensing
items.clue: The change from gas to liquid.

items.label: Melting
items.clue: The change from solid to liquid.

items.label: Compress (squash)
items.clue: To push a substance into a smaller volume.

items.label: Vibrate
items.clue: To move quickly back and forth about a fixed position, as particles in a solid do

questions.stem: Why does a solid, such as a block of iron, keep its own shape?

options.text: Its particles are too hard to bend
Its particles are not moving at all
Iron fills the gaps between its particles
Its particles are held in fixed places

questions.explanation: Yes. Each particle is held in a fixed place, where it can only vibrate. The particles cannot move past each other, so the shape stays the same.

questions.stem: A puddle evaporates on a cool day, far below 100 °C. How is evaporation different from boiling?

options.text: It splits the water into hydrogen and oxygen
It takes place only at the boiling point
It makes a different gas from boiling
It takes place only at the liquid's surface

questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling forms bubbles of gas all through the liquid.

questions.stem: What causes the pressure of the air inside a sealed bottle?

options.text: Air particles hitting all of the walls
Air particles pulling on one another
Air particles packed tight against the walls
Air particles floating up against the lid

questions.explanation: Yes. The air particles move fast in all directions and keep hitting the walls. Each hit is a tiny push, and huge numbers of hits add up to the pressure.

questions.stem: Pure water has been boiling in a beaker for ten minutes. Big bubbles keep forming inside the water. What is in the bubbles?

options.text: Air that was mixed into the water
Water that has turned into a gas
Hydrogen and oxygen from split water
Heat that is escaping from the hot water

questions.explanation: Yes. Boiling happens all through the liquid: water particles break away inside it and form bubbles of water vapour, which rise and escape.

questions.stem: A sealed syringe of air can be pushed in a long way. The same syringe filled with water hardly moves. Why?

options.text: Water particles have water in the gaps
Air particles are soft and squash easily
Air particles have large spaces between them
Air particles are lighter than water ones

questions.explanation: Yes. In air the particles are far apart, so pushing moves them closer together. In water the particles are already touching, so there is almost no space to squash them into.

questions.stem: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. At room temperature it turns straight into a gas. What happens to its particles?

options.text: They each swell up into bigger particles
They break free and spread far and wide
They lose their weight and float away
They are used up and stop existing

questions.explanation: Yes. This is sublimation. The particles break free from the solid and spread far apart as a gas, without becoming a liquid first.

questions.stem: Air is sealed in a syringe. The plunger is pushed in and held still for a minute. Why is the air pressure now higher?

options.text: Its particles have been squashed smaller
Its particles hit the walls more often
Its particles are now touching each other
Its particles only push when it is squashed

questions.explanation: Yes. The same particles are now in a smaller space, so they reach the walls and hit them more often. More hits each second means a higher pressure.

questions.stem: A tray of water is put in a freezer and turns to ice. What happens during freezing?

options.text: Cold flows from the freezer into the water
All of the particles stop moving completely
Each particle freezes into a bit of ice
The water transfers energy to its surroundings

questions.explanation: Yes. The freezer is colder than the water, so energy is transferred from the water to the freezer. Its particles settle into fixed places, where they still vibrate.

questions.stem: Steam is far less dense than liquid water. Which idea from the particle model explains this?

options.text: The particles in steam each have less mass
The particles in steam are much further apart
The particles in steam have each grown a lot bigger
The particles in steam have air in between them

questions.explanation: In a gas the same particles are much further apart, so there is less mass in each unit of volume.

questions.stem: A thin layer of water is left on a glass plate. A day later the plate is dry. What happened to the water particles?

options.text: They only left once the water had boiled
They were used up and no longer exist
They escaped from the surface into the air
They soaked down into the plate itself

questions.explanation: Yes. The fastest-moving particles at the surface of the water escaped into the air as a gas. This is evaporation, and it happens well below 100 °C.

questions.stem: Water can be poured from a jug, but a block of ice cannot. Which explains why a liquid flows?

options.text: Its particles can slide past each other
Its particles are far apart, as in a gas
Its particles are softer than ice particles
Its particles have no forces between them

questions.explanation: Liquid particles stay close together but can move past one another, so a liquid flows.

questions.stem: Steam from a hot shower touches a cold mirror and condenses. What happens to the steam particles?

options.text: They shrink down until they are liquid-sized
They lose energy and stop moving at all
They lose energy and move closer together
They turn into a different kind of particle

questions.explanation: On condensing, particles transfer energy to the cold surface, slow down and move close together.
